editorial.tldr: This thread is a label, not one event: six unrelated items that share the word "detection". It opened with a deepfake-detector explainability paper and a post on evading AI code analysis, moved to log monitoring and a general-purpose anomaly score on Nov 9, then reached agents on Nov 10 with a study of how reliably eval frameworks catch agent failures.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 13 Google Developers Blog post reports how its Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks Google did not write, the thread's first vendor write-up on detecting anomalies in agents.
editorial.why_it_matters: Two engineering questions recur across the items: whether a detector is cheap enough to run where the data lives, and whether it can be trusted once deployed. The two newest items ask the second question of agent tooling, first of eval frameworks and now of a vendor's anomaly detector.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting an agent anomaly detector, check which benchmarks its vendor reports and whether they resemble your agents' tool traces; read the Nov 10 eval-framework comparison before letting one framework gate a release.

beats.headline: Two items question whether deployed detectors can be trusted
beats.summary: One paper compares Grad-CAM faithfulness in centralized versus federated deepfake detection; a Hacker News post catalogs techniques for evading AI source code analysis.

beats.headline: November papers target log monitoring and a new general-purpose anomaly score
beats.summary: LogCDM argues large pretrained log models are hard to deploy on monitoring hosts and offers an interpretable graph-drift alternative; Vendi Anomaly Scores proposes an alternative to density, isolation and distance definitions of an anomaly.

beats.headline: Failure detection moves up the stack to agent evaluation frameworks
beats.summary: A three-phase comparative study tests evaluation frameworks on stability, detection and discovery for LLM-based enterprise analytics agents running multi-tool workflows.

beats.headline: Google scores its Agent Anomaly Detection on third-party benchmarks
beats.summary: The post's framing is external validation: results on benchmarks the team did not author. It is a first-party report, and the thread holds no independent replication.

open_questions: Which third-party benchmarks does Google's Agent Anomaly Detection post use, and has anyone outside Google reproduced the scores?
Which evaluation framework in the Nov 10 comparison detects multi-tool agent failures most reliably, and are its scores stable across repeated runs?
Does federated training measurably reduce Grad-CAM faithfulness in deepfake detectors compared with centralized training?
Does LogCDM match the detection accuracy of BERT-scale or 8B-parameter log models on standard log benchmarks without a GPU at inference time?
Does Vendi Anomaly Scores hold up on high-dimensional embedding data such as LLM traces, or only on the benchmarks the paper reports?
Do any of these papers release code an operator could run against production telemetry?
